description: We are a team of two, into space telescope data, data analysis, and machine learning. We are well versed in data processing languages such as python, and we also have experience in web design. We are a team who strive for perfection, and a high-quality product.
summary:
Driftnet is a website that visualizes an object's motion through the sky as a function of time. Instead of animations of computer-generated planets, it displays real images from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Enter any star name or coordinate, and click and drag to flip between the two SPHEREx images of the same sky from different dates. The stars don't move. But anything that does stands out.

Then used our pipeline to search the skies. Our pipeline has searched more than 500,000 SPHEREx images covering about 3.7% of the sky (1527.3 sq deg) and has tracked more than 750 moving objects. Each object has a public evidence page showing where it was seen, how fast it moved, an orbit estimate, whether two independent catalogs (NASA JPL and IMCCE SkyBoT) already know it, and much more predicted information such as chemical composition, infrared colors, and more.

Since this challenge is about Planet X, we tested that question directly. We put 23,400 simulated objects into real images to measure the limitations of our pipeline. Right now we mostly detect asteroids in the main asteroid belt. Planet X is out of reach for now so we show exactly why and what it would take.
details:
Where the idea came from

Pluto was found in 1930 in a way simple enough to explain to a ten-year-old. Clyde Tombaugh took two photos of the same patch of sky on different nights and flipped back and forth between them. The stars didn't move. One faint dot did.

SPHEREx photographs the whole sky again and again in 102 infrared colors, and all of it is public. The raw material for the same trick now exists for the entire sky. What doesn't exist is an easy way for an ordinary person to use it: the images are large science files in a cloud archive. The challenge asked for a public tool that makes it easy for anyone to see how SPHEREx images change over time. We built that, and then asked the next question: what if software blinked every patch for you and kept a list of everything that moved? That list is Driftnet.

What you can do on the site

  • Look anywhere. Type a star name or coordinates. Driftnet finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, pulls a small cutout of each one live from NASA's archive, lines them up, and lets you blink between dates. The five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855−0714, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) are one click each. For faint targets, you can stack the images along the object's expected motion and watch the signal build.
  • See it move. The home page opens with a real moving object caught between two SPHEREx exposures 13 hours apart, so the first thing a visitor sees is what the challenge asked for.
  • Objects. Every moving object the survey has tracked, searchable in plain language. Each has a report page with its sightings, speed, signal quality, an orbit estimate with its uncertainty, a 60-day prediction, the answer from each catalog, and a section called "what could make this wrong." We also measure many more metrics on the moving objects.
  • Sky map. Every patch we have searched, including the ones where we found nothing. Empty patches are results too.
  • Limits. Measurements of how faint and how slow an object can be before our search misses it, and what that means for Planet X.
  • Ask Driftnet. A guide that answers questions about any object, reads reports aloud, and works in 10 languages.

How it works

  1. Read the data. A Python pipeline reads SPHEREx Level 2 images straight from NASA's public cloud bucket, requesting only the bytes it needs. That is how a two-person student team could process hundreds of thousands of images on free computing.
  2. Find sources. In each image we detect every point of light above 4.5 times the noise and use SPHEREx's own per-pixel quality flags to reject bad pixels and cosmic-ray hits.
  3. Remove what stays still. Anything at the same sky position in other visits is a star or galaxy and is dropped.
  4. Link what moves. The remaining detections are linked into tracks that follow one steady motion across about a day of visits, corrected for SPHEREx's own motion in orbit.
  5. Fit an orbit. Each track gets an orbit estimate by statistical ranging, with 100 alternate orbits to show the uncertainty. A one-day arc cannot pin down an orbit, so we show a distance class and the spread.
  6. Check the catalogs. For every sighting we ask NASA JPL (SBIdent and Horizons) and IMCCE SkyBoT what known object should be there, as seen from SPHEREx. A match must land within 15 arcseconds at every sighting. If the catalogs disagree we show both answers.
  7. Write it up. A language model turns the measurements into a plain-language summary. It only sees measured values. Before anything is shown, the site checks every number against the data and blocks any wording that claims a discovery.

The survey runs automatically along the ecliptic and re-checks objects on a schedule. At submission, Driftnet has searched more than 475,000 SPHEREx images in more than 28,000 patches of sky, found motion in more than 900 of them, and tracks more than 750 objects. All but a few dozen are known asteroids, which is what should happen if the method works.

How we know it works

  • Planted objects. We inserted 23,400 simulated moving objects into real SPHEREx images and ran the same pipeline. It recovered about 92% of objects brighter than AB magnitude 17 moving at typical asteroid speeds (10 to 30 arcseconds per hour). The brightness where we find half of them is AB 17.0 to 17.7. Simulated objects are always labeled and never mixed with real ones.
  • False alarms. In 175.5 square degrees of control fields the pipeline produced 2 false candidates. Rare, but not zero, and we say so.
  • Two catalogs agree. For 20 objects JPL had identified, we asked SkyBoT independently. It agreed on 20 of 20, with a typical position difference of 1.2 arcseconds on a telescope whose pixels are 6.2 arcseconds wide.
  • Expert review. Dr. Tavarez-Brown (PhD, Astronomy, University of Washington) reviewed our method and our Planet X claims. Her advice not to rely on one catalog is why we added the second, and her questions about faint-object sensitivity shaped the Limits page.

The Planet X question, answered honestly

It would have been easy to put "Planet X hunter" on the home page. We tested it instead, and the answer is no, not yet.

A planet 400 to 800 AU away moves so slowly that over the one or two days our search links across, it looks like a star. When we planted objects at Planet X speeds, the pipeline missed them at any brightness. It is also a brightness problem: the planet is predicted at AB magnitude 20 to 23, fainter than a single SPHEREx image reaches.

The Limits page turns that into numbers anyone can read. Today our search could see a Neptune-sized planet out to about 300 AU; the predicted range starts at 400. Stacking many images along a slow orbit, which becomes possible after the survey completes in mid-2027, might reach faint enough, and we mark that as an estimate. The stacking tool on the site is a small working version of that method. We think this is more useful than a claim: it tells the next team where the wall is and what gets over it.

What makes Driftnet creative

  • It searches for you. A viewer shows you the sky. Driftnet has already gone through hundreds of thousands of images and tells you where something moved.
  • It reports its own blind spots. Measured detection limits, false-alarm rate, empty patches, and "what could make this wrong" on every object.
  • It never calls anything new. An unmatched object is labeled as not yet identified. The software enforces this wording, including in AI text.
  • Real orbits with real uncertainty. A 3D view shows the range of orbits that fit, and a 60-day prediction tells an observer where to point.
  • A starting point for follow-up. Unidentified objects come with files in the Minor Planet Center's standard format, so someone with a telescope can check our work. Nothing is submitted automatically.

Who it is for, and the impact we hope for

  • Curious people watch something real move across the sky minutes after first hearing about SPHEREx.
  • Teachers and students get a worked example of how scientists test a claim: detect, check against what is known, measure the error rate, state the limits.
  • Amateur astronomers get positions, predictions and follow-up files for objects worth a second look.
  • Researchers get measured moving-object detection limits for SPHEREx, with open code and data.

SPHEREx keeps scanning, and the survey keeps running on its own, so every data release makes the map bigger without anyone touching it. It works in 10 languages, with read-aloud, voice questions, plain wording, and on a phone.

What we had to consider

  • SPHEREx is not a normal camera. The color it records changes across the detector, so subtracting one image from another creates fake changes. We judge motion by position, not brightness.
  • Big pixels and short arcs. At 6.2 arcseconds per pixel slow objects barely move, and a day of data cannot give a precise orbit. We measured both limits and show the uncertainty everywhere.
  • Catalogs fail. They time out or carry poor orbits. We use two, re-check on a schedule, and say "not checked yet" when a service has not answered.
  • AI can make things up. So AI never finds, measures or identifies anything. It only explains numbers that ordinary code produced, and its output is checked.
  • Cost and access. Everything runs on free tiers. Anyone can fork the repo and run it.

Tools and languages

  • Science pipeline: Python, Astropy, Photutils, NumPy, SciPy, SQLite
  • API: TypeScript, Hono, Cloudflare Workers, Workers KV, D1
  • Website: React, Next.js, hosted on Vercel
  • AI features: Meta Llama, m2m100, MeloTTS and Whisper on Cloudflare Workers AI
  • Automation and testing: GitHub Actions, pytest, Vitest, Playwright, Lighthouse
  • Hardware: none beyond our laptops and free cloud runners

What comes next

Linking detections across weeks and months instead of one day, which is the step that brings slow, distant objects into reach. A larger share of the sky. And, after human vetting, reporting the best unidentified objects to the Minor Planet Center so other telescopes can confirm or rule them out.
